summary.text: A finite check shows that for every \(1\le d\le2025\) one can choose two primes \(p,q\in\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}\) with different final digits, \(p,q\nmid d\), and \(pq\le150\). Since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(pq\), among the first \(pq\) terms of any progression with difference \(d\) one is divisible by both \(p\) and \(q\), so that term has prime divisors with two different final digits.

full_proof.text:
Call an integer \(n>1\) lopsided if all prime divisors of \(n\) have the same final decimal digit. We prove that no arithmetic progression of length \(150\), with positive common difference at most \(2025\), can consist entirely of lopsided numbers.

Suppose, for contradiction, that there are integers \(a,d\) such that
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025,
\]
and every one of
\[
a,\ a+d,\ a+2d,\ldots,\ a+149d
\]
is lopsided.

We will find two small primes \(p,q\) satisfying all of the following:

1. \(p\nmid d\) and \(q\nmid d\);
2. \(p\) and \(q\) have different final decimal digits;
3. \(pq\le 150\).

The finite list of candidate pairs is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(2,11),(2,13),\\
&(3,5),(3,7),(3,11),(3,17),\\
&(5,7),(5,11),(5,13),\\
&(7,11),(7,13),(11,13).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
Every number appearing here is prime. The products of the pairs, in the same order, are
\[
6,10,14,22,26,15,21,33,51,35,55,65,77,91,143,
\]
so every product is at most \(150\). Moreover, the two primes in each listed pair have different residues modulo \(10\). Thus it remains only to prove that, for every \(d\le 2025\), at least one pair in (1) consists of two primes that do not divide \(d\).

We give the complete finite argument for that assertion. Form a graph whose vertices are
\[
V=\{2,3,5,7,11,13,17\}
\]
and whose edges are exactly the fifteen pairs in (1). Let
\[
N=\{r\in V:r\nmid d\}
\]
be the set of these seven primes that do not divide \(d\). If no edge of the graph had both endpoints in \(N\), then \(N\) would be an independent set.

The maximal independent sets of this graph are precisely
\[
\{2,17\},\quad \{3,13\},\quad \{5,17\},\quad
\{7,17\},\quad \{11,17\},\quad \{13,17\}.
\tag{2}
\]
Here is a direct check of this classification. The vertex \(17\) is joined only to \(3\). Among the other five vertices
\[
\{2,5,7,11,13\},
\]
every pair is an edge. Therefore an independent set containing \(17\) cannot contain \(3\) and can contain at most one of those other five vertices. Its maximal possibilities are consequently the five sets
\[
\{2,17\},\{5,17\},\{7,17\},\{11,17\},\{13,17\}.
\]
If an independent set does not contain \(17\), consider the six vertices
\(\{2,3,5,7,11,13\}\). Every pair among these is an edge except \((3,13)\). Hence the only maximal independent set in this part of the graph is \(\{3,13\}\). This proves (2).

Every independent set is contained in a maximal independent set, so if \(N\) were independent, it would be contained in one of the six sets in (2). Every prime outside that maximal independent set would then divide \(d\). Since these primes are distinct, their product would divide \(d\). The complementary products corresponding to the six sets in (2) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{maximal independent set }M&V\setminus M&\displaystyle\prod_{r\in V\setminus M}r\\ \hline
\{2,17\}&\{3,5,7,11,13\}&15015\\
\{3,13\}&\{2,5,7,11,17\}&13090\\
\{5,17\}&\{2,3,7,11,13\}&6006\\
\{7,17\}&\{2,3,5,11,13\}&4290\\
\{11,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,13\}&2730\\
\{13,17\}&\{2,3,5,7,11\}&2310.
\end{array}
\]
In every case, \(d\) would be divisible by an integer at least \(2310\). Because \(d>0\), this would imply \(d\ge2310\), contrary to \(d\le2025\). Thus \(N\) is not independent. Consequently, some edge \((p,q)\) from (1) has both endpoints in \(N\). In other words,
\[
p\nmid d,\qquad q\nmid d.
\]
As already noted, this pair also satisfies \(pq\le150\) and \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\).

Because \(p\) and \(q\) are distinct primes and neither divides \(d\), we have
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1.
\]
Therefore \(d\) has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(pq\). Choose the unique residue class \(i\pmod{pq}\) satisfying
\[
i\equiv -a d^{-1}\pmod{pq},
\]
and take its representative with
\[
0\le i<pq.
\]
Then
\[
a+id\equiv a-a d^{-1}d\equiv0\pmod{pq}.
\]
Thus both \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\).

Since \(pq\le150\), the chosen index satisfies
\[
0\le i<pq\le150,
\]
so \(i\) is one of \(0,1,\ldots,149\). Hence \(a+id\) is one of the asserted \(150\) lopsided terms. Also \(a+id\ge a\ge2\), so its prime divisors are well-defined in the usual nontrivial sense. But it has the two prime divisors \(p\) and \(q\), and these have different final decimal digits because
\[
p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}.
\]
Therefore \(a+id\) is not lopsided, a contradiction.

It follows that there do not exist integers \(a\ge2\) and \(1\le d\le2025\) for which all \(150\) terms \(a+id\), \(0\le i<150\), have all their prime divisors ending in the same decimal digit. This disproves the conjecture.
